small_guidance:
- Add larger tile configs tailored to M=N=K=8192 on Ada (e.g., `BLOCK_M=128, BLOCK_N=256, BLOCK_K=64, num_warps=8, num_stages=3` and `BLOCK_M=256, BLOCK_N=128, BLOCK_K=64, num_warps=8, num_stages=3`); the K=8192 inner loop benefits from `num_stages=3-4` to overlap loads with `tl.dot`.
- Cast accumulator output to fp16/bf16 only if needed; here keep fp32 but ensure A/B loads use `tl.multiple_of`/`tl.max_contiguous` hints on the contiguous axes to improve vectorization. Also try `GROUP_M=4` and `GROUP_M=16` — for 8192/128 = 64 row-tiles, 8 may not be optimal for L2 reuse.
- Mask the K-loop tail only when `K % BLOCK_K != 0`; here 8192 is divisible by all BLOCK_K so loads can stay unmasked (already the case). Add `tl.assume(K % BLOCK_K == 0)` style boundary-free configs and consider an `EVEN_K: tl.constexpr` flag.
large_guidance:
- Switch to a split-K or persistent-CTA GEMM: with M=N=8192 there are 64×64=4096 output tiles for 128×128 — well above SM count, so persistent kernels reduce launch/scheduling overhead and allow software pipelining of the long K=8192 reduction.
- Consider running in TF32 (`tl.dot(a, b, allow_tf32=True)` with input cast) — the 5e-2 tolerance easily admits TF32, and on Ada/Ampere TF32 doubles matmul throughput vs fp32 dot. Fuse the dual-Mish epilogue exactly as today.
- Alternatively, store weight as fp16/bf16 once at init and run a mixed-precision GEMM (fp16 inputs, fp32 accumulate); this halves global-memory traffic for the B matrix (8192×8192×4B = 256MB → 128MB) which is currently the bandwidth bottleneck.
